name: biogears-sbml-sepsis
title: Simulation core — one sepsis model, every engine: composed, ensembled, orchestrated, benchmarked

campaign_docs.name: BioGears sepsis core in Antimony: extraction report (Sauro)
campaign_docs.path: investigations/biogears-sbml-sepsis/sources/BioGears sepsis core in Antimony extraction report.pdf

lead:
The simulation core takes one specification — the BioGears sepsis core, a
lumped-parameter whole-body physiology model (cardiovascular circuit, baroreflex,
capillary fluid/albumin exchange, and the McDaniel 2019 Acute Inflammatory
Response) — and runs it under interchangeable engines behind one typed interface:
the original BioGears 8.2.0 C++ engine (viva-biogears), the exact SBML/Antimony
extraction integrated by roadrunner/CVODE (viva-tellurium), and a learned PyTorch
surrogate (viva-torch). Because each engine is a box over the same observable
ports, the core can compose them into workflows, sweep them as ensembles, pass a
model artifact from one to another, profile their compute, run the same composite
under a Rust backend, and couple two engines in a closed loop. This investigation
puts those capabilities in front of the INFLECT team, each as something you can
open and run.

at_a_glance.role: REPRESENT / start here — the one model, its engines, and the capabilities this investigation demonstrates.
INTERCHANGEABILITY — which model properties survive an implementation swap (BioGears, Tellurium, surrogate); a common port layout does not guarantee equal physiology.
EXPLORE — a severity × engine batch as one sweep, probing progression toward shock.
ORCHESTRATE — registered modules form a reproducible pipeline with no new integration code, handing an SBML file between engines and fanning the composite across a Nextflow severity grid.

SCALE — where acceleration preserves useful predictions and where it fails; the stiff-ODE cost, the ~40,000× surrogate tier, the Rust (viva-core) backend, and COPASI as a second exact-SBML engine that reproduces Tellurium at ~4.7× the cost.
EXPLAIN — the engines agree on the inflammation core to within ~0.1% and diverge in the hemodynamic layer; the discrepancy to investigate.
INTERVENE — physiology coupled to a treatment process every tick; untreated vs early vs delayed, with a coupling-step convergence test.
VALIDATE — the Workbench turning runs into traceable evidence with explicit pass / fail / pending acceptance criteria.
REDUCE — drop the per-beat event for a continuous mean-hemodynamics model: ~10^7x faster and engine-agnostic, at a stated fidelity cost (speed vs fidelity).

how_to_read:
How the simulation core works, in one idea: a simulation is a COMPOSITE — a small
graph of PROCESSES and STEPS that read and write a shared, TYPED state. Each box in
the graph declares typed input and output ports; the core wires the boxes together
by matching ports to shared state paths and advances them in time. Because the
interface is the ports — not the engine behind them — any engine that exposes the
same observable ports is a drop-in. That is the whole trick: the BioGears sepsis
core is ONE specification, and three different engines are each wrapped as a box
over the same ports —
  - BioGearsProcess   — the original BioGears 8.2.0 C++ physiology engine;
  - TelluriumUTCStep  — the exact SBML/Antimony extraction, integrated by roadrunner (CVODE);
  - NeuralProcess     — a learned PyTorch surrogate of the same core.
Swapping engines is swapping ONE box's address. The wiring, the emitters that record
results, and the analysis are all unchanged. "Same spec, many engines" is not a
slogan here — it is what the typed-port interface buys you (study 01).

How the orchestration works, in four verbs: the unified workflow API exposes exactly
this over HTTP, thinly — every call just builds and runs a composite.
  1. LIST modules       (GET /modules)              — the registered boxes you can use.
  2. RUN one module     (POST /modules/{name}/call) — run one box as a 1-node composite.
  3. CONNECT a workflow (POST /workflows)           — a composite spec: nodes (boxes) + wires.
  4. RUN the workflow   (POST /workflows/{id}/run)  — advance the composite, read the outputs.
Study 03 is the running example: it connects modules into a pipeline and hands the
Antimony/SBML extraction from one engine to another. Study 02 runs the engines as an
ensemble; study 04 profiles where each spends compute. Full reference:
docs/workflow-api.md and docs/api.md.

glossary.definition: A runnable simulation: a graph of processes/steps wired through a shared typed state. The core advances it in time.

A box in the composite. A PROCESS advances one time interval per update (e.g. BioGears, the surrogate); a STEP runs once to completion (e.g. a full Tellurium time course, a math derivation). Both expose typed input/output ports.
The named, typed inputs and outputs a box declares. Engines that expose the same ports are interchangeable — this is why one sepsis spec runs under three engines by swapping one box.
A registered process/step, addressable by name (e.g. TelluriumUTCStep, NeuralProcess). Dozens are registered (this workspace lists 76 at GET /modules).
A composite built through the API: a list of nodes (modules) plus wires connecting one node's output port to another's input port.

list a module, run one module, connect modules into a workflow, run the workflow — the entire workflow API surface (GET /modules, POST /modules/{name}/call, POST /workflows, POST /workflows/{id}/run).
Running many configurations (here severity × engine) as one orchestrated batch and gathering their endpoints into a single comparison.
A learned neural approximation (viva-torch NeuralProcess) of an engine's per-step dynamics. Replaces the ODE solve with one forward pass: ~4-5 orders of magnitude faster, approximate.

biological_story:
Sepsis in BioGears is a race between an inflammatory response and the
cardiovascular system that keeps blood pressure up. A bacterial load seeds the
tissue; the Acute Inflammatory Response (McDaniel 2019) amplifies, tissue integrity
falls, capillaries leak, and fluid moves from blood to interstitium. The heart and
vasculature compensate — heart rate and vascular tone rise — until, in severe
sepsis, that compensation fatigues and pressure falls toward septic shock.

This is the model the simulation core runs under every engine. The inflammation half
of the race the SBML extraction translates faithfully: run against the real engine,
tissue integrity and pathogen load track it to within ~0.1% in both mild and
severe infection. The cardiovascular half is where the engines part — BioGears
carries a whole driven body (nutrition schedule, temperature, respiration, renal
fluid handling, nitric-oxide and fever vasodilation, continuous baroreflex control),
so even a controlled infection shows pressures wandering over ~10 mmHg, while the
autonomous extraction holds those inputs at baseline and traces smooth. Same clinical
outcome, different hemodynamic path to shock — the measured fidelity limit in study 05,
which is why the capabilities here are shown on a model whose edges are stated, not hidden.
question:
How can a compositional simulation core support interchangeable physiological
models, systematic perturbation studies, scalable execution, mechanistic
comparison, dynamic intervention, and evidence-based scientific validation? Taking
one real model, the BioGears sepsis core, each is a runnable artifact:
  01 INTERCHANGEABILITY — which model properties are preserved when the
     implementation changes (BioGears C++, extracted SBML/Tellurium, surrogate)?
  02 ENSEMBLES — how do severity and physiological parameters drive progression
     toward shock?
  03 ORCHESTRATION — can registered modules form a reproducible investigation with
     no new integration code, including inside a Nextflow pipeline?
  04 SCALABLE EXECUTION — where does acceleration preserve useful predictions, and
     where does it fail? Includes the Rust viva-core backend.
  05 MECHANISTIC FIDELITY — what explains the inflammatory agreement and the
     hemodynamic divergence between engines?
  06 DYNAMIC COUPLING — can coupled physiology and treatment produce consistent
     intervention responses (untreated vs early vs delayed)?
  07 EVIDENCE & ACCEPTANCE — can the Workbench turn runs into traceable evidence
     with explicit pass / fail / pending acceptance criteria?
The showcase is about what the core lets scientists test, not only what software it
can execute — while staying honest about where the engines agree and where they do not.
hypothesis:
This is a capabilities demonstration, not a single hypothesis test. The claim is
that the simulation core already does all of the above on a real model, with each
capability shown by an artifact that runs. The one genuine hypothesis is in the
fidelity backbone (study 05): the SBML extraction reproduces the inflammation core
to within ~0.1% but diverges from the BioGears engine in the hemodynamic layer. That
is a real, measured result, and it keeps the demonstration credible.

executive.what_is_this:
A guided tour of the simulation core's capabilities on one real model. The same
BioGears sepsis core is run under interchangeable engines (BioGears C++, two exact
SBML integrators — Tellurium and COPASI — a PyTorch surrogate, and a Rust execution
backend) and used to
demonstrate, each as a runnable artifact: COMPOSITION (study 01 — the same spec
under three engines by one node swap), ENSEMBLES (study 02 — a severity × engine
batch in one sweep), ORCHESTRATION/WORKFLOWS (study 03 — the four-verb API composes
modules into a pipeline and hands an Antimony/SBML file between engines, and a
Nextflow pipeline fans the real composite across a severity grid), PERFORMANCE &
EXECUTION BACKENDS (study 04 — where the compute goes, a ~40,000× surrogate tier,
and the same composite run under the Rust viva-core backend), and CO-SIMULATION
(study 06 — two processes exchanging state every tick: the physiology engine
coupled to a closed-loop antibiotic controller, with untreated/early/delayed arms),
and EVIDENCE & ACCEPTANCE (study 07 — turning runs into traceable pass/fail/pending
acceptance criteria). A fidelity backbone (study 05) keeps it honest: where the
engines agree, and where they do not.
executive.verdict:
The simulation core does all of this. One sepsis spec runs under three
interchangeable engines by swapping a single box (01). A severity × engine batch
runs as one sweep (02). The four-verb workflow API composes registered modules into
a pipeline and passes the SBML extraction from one engine to another with no new
simulation code, and a Nextflow pipeline fans the same composite across a severity
grid (03). The same run spans 4+ orders of magnitude of compute — BioGears ~3.38 h,
Tellurium ~2.81 h, the surrogate ~0.2 s — spent almost entirely in the stiff
91-state ODE solve the surrogate replaces with one forward pass, and the same
composite also runs under the Rust viva-core backend (04). Two processes exchange
state every tick in a closed loop: an antibiotic controller coupled to the sepsis
engine clears the pathogen, and early beats delayed treatment (06). The Workbench
then turns these runs into traceable acceptance criteria — the inflammation gates
pass, a hemodynamic gate fails, and a surrogate-accuracy gate is left pending (07).
The demonstration stays honest (05): the extraction reproduces the inflammation core
to within ~0.1% but reaches septic shock by a different hemodynamic mechanism and on
a flipped timeline, and the surrogate is fast but not admissible on the severe arm.
executive.verdict_detail:
Each capability is a runnable artifact in its study: the engine overlay (01), the
severity × engine ensemble grid (02), the hand-off workflow and its DAG plus the
Nextflow pipeline (03), the compute profile and live per-step micro-benchmark and
the Rust-backend run and the surrogate admissibility check (04), the closed-loop
co-simulation with treatment counterfactuals and a convergence test (06), and the
acceptance-gate evaluation (07). Heavy full runs (BioGears ~3.38 h, Tellurium
~2.81 h) are cited from committed wall-clock; the cheaper demonstrations run live.
The fidelity backbone (05) carries the measured engine-vs-extraction comparison
(inflammation near-identical at ~0.1%; hemodynamics diverge in mechanism and
timing), so the capabilities are shown on a model whose limits are stated, not hidden.
decisions_needed: Follow-up (05, staged): test one candidate mechanism for the hemodynamic divergence (e.g. a simplified vasodilatory effect) with a controlled perturbation; quantify whether it reduces the time-to-shock discrepancy. Do not present documented omissions as proven causes.

Follow-up (02, staged): a 5×5 severity × physiology-parameter sweep with time-to-hypotension, minimum MAP, and tissue integrity — an actual biological response surface (compute-heavy on the stiff engine).
Follow-up (01, partial): a port / units / initialization / ownership compatibility report across the three implementations.
Follow-up (03, partial): automated shock-event detection and metric extraction as a reusable workflow step.
Done this pass (06): untreated vs early vs delayed treatment counterfactuals + a coupling-step convergence test.
Done this pass (04): surrogate admissibility on a withheld severity (screening-grade vs mechanistic).
Done this pass (07): pass / fail / pending acceptance gates linked to evidence artifacts.

scientific_argument.main_claim:
Vivarium is a shared computational architecture for executing, composing, and
investigating physiological models. Using a BioGears-derived sepsis model, the
showcase examines model interchangeability, simulation ensembles, interoperable
workflows, accelerated execution, mechanistic discrepancy, closed-loop intervention,
and evidence-based acceptance. Each capability answers a biological question,
produces a runnable artifact, and carries a scoped evidence verdict. The story runs
Represent -> Explore -> Orchestrate -> Scale -> Explain -> Intervene -> Validate.
Together these establish a foundation for INFLECT's broader adaptive physiological
modeling goals, without inflating the demonstration into a patient-specific digital
twin.
evidence_for: COMPOSITION: one sepsis spec runs under BioGears, Tellurium, and the surrogate by swapping one box; the shared observables overlay (study 01).
ENSEMBLES: a severity {0,1,3} × engine batch runs as one orchestrated sweep into a single grid (study 02).

ORCHESTRATION/WORKFLOWS: the four verbs compose registered modules into a pipeline and hand the Antimony/SBML extraction between engines; a Nextflow pipeline fans the real sepsis composite across a severity grid — no new simulation code (study 03).

PERFORMANCE & EXECUTION BACKENDS: one 48 h run spans BioGears ~3.38 h / Tellurium ~2.81 h / surrogate ~0.2 s; a live per-step micro-benchmark confirms the stiff-ODE bottleneck; the same composite runs under the Rust viva-core backend with matching results; the surrogate leaves physical bounds on 8 of 9 severe observables (study 04).

CO-SIMULATION: two processes in one composite exchange state every tick — the sepsis physiology engine coupled to a closed-loop antibiotic controller that senses bacteremia and writes the drug-killed pathogen back into the engine, clearing it relative to the matched untreated control; untreated/early/delayed arms and a coupling-step convergence test (study 06).

EVIDENCE & ACCEPTANCE: pre-declared acceptance criteria evaluate against committed evidence to 2 pass / 1 fail / 1 pending, each linked to its artifact — the inflammation gates pass, the hemodynamic gate fails, the surrogate-accuracy gate is pending (study 07).
evidence_against: Fidelity limit: the extraction reaches MAP<65 shock by a different hemodynamic mechanism and ~15 h earlier than the engine despite lagging ~11 h on systolic pressure (study 05).
The surrogate is an approximate tier — bounded over the full horizon but not yet clinically accurate; it trades accuracy for ~4-5 orders of magnitude of speed (study 04).
Engine fluctuates continuously (nutrition schedule, full homeostatic control) while the autonomous extraction is near-flat — same outcome, no ambient life (study 05).
caveats: Heavy full-run wall-clocks (BioGears, Tellurium) are cited from committed runs, not re-measured in this redesign; the new ensemble/workflow/micro-benchmark artifacts run live.
'Functional-difference' attributions (study 05) come from the extraction report's own 'Differences from BioGears' inventory — documented omissions, not newly-measured mechanisms.
The surrogate is trained on the sepsis SBML core (98 observables, 300 s step); it is an approximate tier, not a validated clinical model.

studies.name: 00-simulation-core
studies.title: The Simulation Core — a composable foundation for physiological modeling
studies.question:
What can the simulation core do? This investigation takes ONE real model — the
BioGears sepsis core — and shows four capabilities on it, each as something you
can open and run, not a claim on a slide:
  1. COMPOSITION  — run the same spec under interchangeable engines (study 01).
  2. ENSEMBLES    — run a severity × engine batch in one orchestrated sweep (study 02).
  3. ORCHESTRATION / WORKFLOWS — compose modules into a pipeline and hand an
     Antimony/SBML file between engines (study 03).
  4. PERFORMANCE  — profile where the compute goes and how fast each engine is (study 04).
A fidelity backbone (study 05) keeps it honest: where the engines agree, and where
they do not.

findings.summary: One model, every engine — the same sepsis spec runs under three interchangeable engines by swapping one box.
findings.detail:
The BioGears sepsis core is ONE specification. Each engine is a box over the
same typed observable ports, so swapping engines is swapping one node address —
the wiring, the emitters, and the analysis are unchanged:
  - BioGearsProcess — the original BioGears 8.2.0 C++ physiology engine;
  - TelluriumUTCStep / TelluriumProcess — the exact SBML/Antimony extraction, integrated by roadrunner (CVODE);
  - NeuralProcess — a learned PyTorch surrogate of the same core.
This is the composition pillar; study 01 shows the three engines side by side.
findings.statement: Swapping engines means changing one typed node address. This shows the engines are interchangeable at the port boundary. It does not claim the three produce the same physiology.
findings.explanation:
This finding sets up the composition pillar the rest of the investigation stands on. The evidence is structural, not a single measured number. One sepsis spec exposes a fixed set of typed observable ports. Each engine sits as one node behind those ports: the BioGears 8.2.0 C++ physiology engine, the exact SBML/Antimony extraction integrated by roadrunner/CVODE (Tellurium), and the learned PyTorch surrogate. Moving between engines changes one node address; the wiring, emitters, and downstream analysis stay fixed.

The downstream artifacts show the swap is real. On the committed 72 h severe-arm run, study 01 records the inflammation core (tissue integrity, blood pathogen) overlapping to within ~0.1% between the two full-physics engines, and the surrogate completing a full 576-step rollout in a fraction of a second. Three independently built engines drive the same spec through the same ports. Study 02 varies severity x engine, study 03 hands an Antimony/SBML file between engines, and study 04 profiles each one.

Interchangeable means drop-in at the typed port boundary, not numerically equal. Study 05 is qualified on exactly this line: the engines reach baseline parity and a near-identical inflammation core, but their hemodynamic layers differ in mechanism and timing. The surrogate makes this clearest. Study 04 records a ~40,000x full-run (~13,000x per-step) speedup over the stiff ODE solve, but that is a cost claim only; it works as a drop-in replacement only once the fidelity gate is met, and that number lives in study 05.

Limitation: this finding has no numeric observed value, and should not. Its evidence is that the downstream studies exist and run, not a measured scalar. It is a demonstration-level claim about the artifacts, not a validation of their physiology. Two things stay open: the hemodynamic MAP/HR/SVR trajectories, where the two full-physics engines disagree in mechanism and timing, and the test that would settle them — a pre-registered discriminating test against an external hemodynamic reference. Study 05 bounds the divergence but cannot yet say which engine is right. Until that test exists, read this as an inventory of runnable, port-compatible capability over one spec, not as evidence that any engine reproduces real sepsis hemodynamics.

findings.summary: The four pillars, each a runnable study.
findings.detail:
- COMPOSITION (study 01): the same spec under three engines, one node swapped.
- ENSEMBLES (study 02): a severity × engine batch run as one orchestrated sweep.
- ORCHESTRATION / WORKFLOWS (study 03): the four-verb API composes modules into a
  pipeline and hands an Antimony/SBML file between engines.
- PERFORMANCE (study 04): where the compute goes (stiff ODE), and the surrogate's
  ~40,000× speedup.
- FIDELITY (study 05): where the engines agree, and where they do not — so the
  demonstration stays credible.
findings.statement: The four capability pillars plus the fidelity backbone are each a study you can open and run, not a slide assertion. Together they map what the core can do, ordered so each study builds on the last. The map does not validate any pillar's physiology.
findings.explanation:
This finding is the investigation's map. Each capability the core claims is a study you can open and run, and the studies depend on one another in order. Composition (study 01) comes first: it sets up the one thing everything else reuses — the same sepsis spec behind one typed port boundary, with the engine as a single swappable node (the sibling finding on one-model-every-engine says the same). Ensembles (study 02) runs a severity x engine batch over that interchange. Workflows (study 03) hands an Antimony/SBML file between those engines through the four-verb API. Performance (study 04) profiles where the compute goes on the same spec, including the fast approximate surrogate tier. The pillars are one interchange shown four ways, so the order composition -> ensembles -> workflows -> performance is part of the claim, not just a list.

The fidelity backbone (study 05) sits outside that chain. It bounds all four and keeps 'each pillar runs' from being read as 'each pillar is physiologically correct'. The engines reach baseline parity and a near-identical inflammation core but diverge on the hemodynamic layer in mechanism and timing, which is why study 05's verdict is qualified, not supported. That qualification carries upward: the surrogate speedup in study 04 is a per-step compute result bounded by study 05's agreement envelope, and the ensemble and workflow pillars inherit the same ceiling. The map is only as strong as its weakest link, not as strong as the number of runnable studies.

Limitation: this finding has no numeric observed value, and should not. Its evidence is structural — the five downstream studies exist and run — not a measured quantity. No single metric grades 'the core does all four'; the claim is checked study by study. Open question: there is no pre-registered discriminating test that would turn this map from 'four capabilities demonstrated over one spec' into 'four capabilities validated against an external reference', most sharply on the hemodynamic layer where study 05 records divergence but cannot yet say which engine is right. Until that test exists, read this as an inventory of runnable capability, not evidence that any pillar reproduces real sepsis physiology.

studies.claim:
The simulation core runs one sepsis specification under three interchangeable
engines: BioGears (C++ physiology), Tellurium (exact SBML via roadrunner/CVODE),
and a PyTorch surrogate. It composes and orchestrates them into workflows (including
passing an Antimony/SBML file between engines), runs them as ensembles, and does so
performantly (seconds to hours across engines; a ~40,000× surrogate tier). Every
capability below is a runnable artifact. The surrogate is a fast approximate tier —
bounded, not yet clinically accurate — not a drop-in replacement.

derived.insight: Swapping engines means changing one typed node address. This shows the engines are interchangeable at the port boundary. It does not claim the three produce the same physiology.

studies.name: 01-composition
studies.title: Model Interchangeability — one physiological specification, multiple implementations
studies.question:
Does the same sepsis specification run under interchangeable engines by swapping
one box — BioGears (C++ physiology), the exact SBML extraction (Tellurium/CVODE),
and a PyTorch surrogate — all through one typed-port interface?

parent_studies.rationale: Interchangeability needs the shared core and the one sepsis model.

findings.summary: One sepsis spec, two full-physics engines overlaid on nine observables — same spec, one box swapped.
findings.detail:
The same BioGears sepsis core specification runs under the BioGears 8.2.0 C++
engine and under the exact SBML/Antimony extraction (Tellurium/roadrunner,
CVODE). Across all nine shared observables the inflammation core (tissue
integrity, blood pathogen) overlaps to within ~0.1%; the hemodynamic observables
diverge (studied in 05). Because each engine is a box over the same typed
observable ports, the swap is a single node-address change — nothing else in
the composite moves.
findings.statement: The same sepsis spec runs under interchangeable engines. The two full-physics engines agree on the inflammation core — that is the composition proof. They diverge on the hemodynamic layer, which study 05 is set up to settle. The surrogate is interchangeable at the interface; its accuracy is deferred to study 04.
findings.explanation:
Agreement and divergence here mean different things, and both matter. On the committed 72 h severe-arm run, the inflammation core — tissue integrity and blood pathogen — overlaps to within ~0.1% between the BioGears 8.2.0 C++ engine and the exact SBML/Antimony extraction integrated by Tellurium/roadrunner (CVODE). Two independently built full-physics engines reproduce the same spec through the same typed observable ports. That overlap is the composition proof: swapping the engine changes one node's address and nothing else in the composite — wiring, emitters, and analysis are untouched (report-card axes tellurium_builds and surrogate_runs are both within_tol over the real 91-state model).

The PyTorch surrogate is interchangeable in the same structural way. It constructs over that 91-state model and completes a full 576-step rollout in 0.198 s (engines_live_check.json). But that is interchangeability of interface, not accuracy; its output is bounded yet out of range, which is why its claim is speed (study 04), not fidelity.

The two full-physics engines diverge on the hemodynamic layer. That divergence is not a flaw in the composition; it is the signal this study hands downstream. The open question is which engine's MAP/HR/SVR trajectories to trust, and study 05 is set up to settle it. This is the first link of the chain the investigation builds on: composition shows one spec runs under swappable engines, which ensembles (02) vary, workflows (03) orchestrate, performance (04) times, and fidelity (05) judges. Honest limit: the ~0.1% figure is an authored reading of a single committed severe-arm run reused from study 03, not a seed ensemble and not a code-graded band, so it demonstrates that the engines agree on the inflammation core rather than giving a calibrated error bound.

findings.summary: The surrogate is the third interchangeable engine — it constructs and runs live here.
findings.detail:
The PyTorch surrogate (viva-torch NeuralProcess) is the same sepsis core as a
learned box over the same ports. The live check (engines_live_check.json)
confirms it: the Tellurium/roadrunner engine constructs over the real 91-state
model, and the surrogate runs a full 48 h / 576-step rollout in a fraction of a
second, finite (though out of physical range — it is degenerate across severity).
It is a fast APPROXIMATE tier — not asserted
clinically accurate (its speed is study 04; the honest accuracy picture is 05).
findings.statement: The PyTorch surrogate is the third interchangeable engine at the interface. It constructs over the same 91-state sepsis spec and completes a full 48 h / 576-step rollout live (0.198 s, finite but out of physical range). Swapping to it is one node-address change, like swapping BioGears for exact Tellurium. That is interchangeability of interface; speed is deferred to study 04 and accuracy to study 05.
findings.explanation:
This finding shows interchangeability of interface, not accuracy, and the honest work is saying which. In the live check (engines_live_check.json) the Tellurium/roadrunner engine constructs over the real 91-state SBML extraction, and the PyTorch surrogate (viva-torch NeuralProcess) completes a full 48 h / 576-step rollout in 0.198 s with finite output. The learned box plugs into the same typed observable ports as the two full-physics engines and runs end to end on the one spec. That is the third leg of the composition claim: swapping to the surrogate changes one node's address and nothing else in the composite — wiring, emitters, and analysis are untouched — just like swapping between BioGears and exact Tellurium.

But the surrogate's output, while bounded and finite over the horizon, is out of physical range and degenerate across severity. So the check shows the learned box fits the socket, not that it reproduces the physiology. Its two numeric claims are deferred by design: its speed (the 0.198 s rollout) is study 04, and whether its trajectories can be trusted at all is study 05. In the chain, this finding gives performance (04) and fidelity (05) a surrogate to time and to judge: composition shows a learned engine is swappable at the interface, and the downstream studies decide what that swap costs. Honest limit: interchangeable here is a structural existence claim backed by a single live construction-and-rollout check, not a graded accuracy band. The surrogate is known to be out of physical range, so no fidelity or clinical-accuracy claim is made.

findings.summary: COPASI is a second interchangeable exact-SBML engine — it reproduces Tellurium's trajectory (cross-engine agreement in study 04).
findings.detail:
Beyond the three engines overlaid here, the exact-SBML tier itself is
interchangeable. The identical SBML runs under Tellurium (roadrunner/CVODE, the
main engine) AND under COPASI (LSODA), and the two independent integrators produce
the same severe-arm trajectory — agreeing to a maximum relative difference of ~5e-4
across all nine observables (study 04, chart 03). So the exact-SBML result is a
property of the model, not of any one integrator, which strengthens the fidelity
backbone: when study 05 compares the SBML extraction to the BioGears engine, the
SBML side is cross-validated by two engines. Tellurium stays the main engine; COPASI
runs the same box at a few times the cost (study 04).

studies.claim:
The same sepsis core runs under three interchangeable engines — BioGears (C++),
Tellurium (exact SBML via roadrunner/CVODE), and a PyTorch surrogate — each a box
over the same typed observable ports. Swapping engines is swapping one box's
address. The nine-observable overlay shows the two full-physics engines (BioGears
and exact Tellurium) run the same spec and track to within ~0.1% on the inflammation
core; the surrogate is the third interchangeable engine (its speed and approximate
behavior are study 04). Where the full-physics engines diverge — the hemodynamic
layer — is the fidelity backbone (study 05).

derived.insight: The same sepsis spec runs under interchangeable engines. The two full-physics engines agree on the inflammation core — that is the composition proof. They diverge on the hemodynamic layer, which study 05 is set up to settle. The surrogate is interchangeable at the interface; its accuracy is deferred to study 04.

studies.name: 02-ensembles
studies.title: Simulation Ensembles — systematic perturbation and comparative physiology
studies.question:
Can the simulation core run the sepsis model as an ENSEMBLE — many configurations
(severity × engine) executed as one orchestrated batch and gathered into a single
comparison?

parent_studies.rationale: Ensembles sweep the interchangeable spec across severity and engine.

findings.summary: One batch, severity × engine — the full-physics engines show the severity response and agree.
findings.detail:
Minimum tissue integrity (the inflammation core) across severities {0,1,3}:
BioGears and the exact Tellurium extraction both fall 1.00 (healthy) -> 0.968
(mild) -> 0.243 (severe), to within ~0.1%. These are the committed heavy runs from the
severity studies (01/02/03), assembled here as one ensemble grid — the same shape
the batch harness produces for any registered engine.

findings.summary: The surrogate ran live across every cell — the orchestration proof.
findings.detail:
In the same batch the PyTorch surrogate was swept across all three severities
live (seconds total), demonstrating that the orchestration runs many cheap
configurations in one sweep. The surrogate is a fast APPROXIMATE tier: its
tissue-integrity endpoint is out of physical range (accuracy is data-limited),
so it is reported for transparency but not presented as a science value. Its
real contribution is speed (study 04); its honest fidelity picture is study 05.
findings.statement: The surrogate's divergence from the full-physics engines is a difference in tier, not a rival prediction. One batch answers a fidelity question and an orchestration question side by side.
findings.explanation:
The batch makes two different kinds of claim, and the apparent divergence sits entirely at the boundary between them. BioGears and the exact Tellurium extraction — two independently built full-physics engines — agree to within ~0.1% on minimum tissue integrity across severities {0,1,3} (1.00 healthy -> 0.968 mild -> 0.243 severe). Because they are separate implementations, that agreement is cross-engine replication: the severity response is a property of the shared model, not an artifact of one engine. That is the fidelity claim this study supports.

The surrogate is a different tier. Its tissue-integrity endpoint is out of physical range, so it is not a third physical estimate competing with the full-physics pair; reading it that way would be wrong. Its presence in every cell proves only what it is meant to: the harness orchestrates many cheap configurations in one sweep (the throughput claim, quantified in study 04). The divergence is by design, not an unresolved contradiction. The full-physics engines answer 'does the model show the expected, engine-independent severity response?' (yes); the surrogate answers 'can the batch harness fan a cheap engine across the whole grid live?' (yes). Neither bears on the other.

The open question the divergence makes visible is whether the surrogate can be moved from orchestration-proof to a science-grade tier at all. This grid cannot decide that; it needs a held-out quantitative fidelity test for the surrogate against the full-physics endpoints, which is the work deferred to study 05. Until that test exists, the surrogate's number stays reported for transparency and excluded from any fidelity claim.

studies.claim:
The sepsis core runs as a severity {0,1,3} × engine {BioGears, Tellurium, surrogate}
ensemble, gathered into one grid. The two full-physics engines agree to within ~0.1% and
show the expected severity response (minimum tissue integrity 1.00 healthy -> 0.97
mild -> 0.24 severe); their heavy runs are cited from the committed severity studies.
The surrogate ran live across every cell in the same batch — the orchestration proof
that the harness executes many cheap configurations in one sweep — and is flagged a
fast approximate tier (its endpoint is out of physical range; its real contribution,
speed, is study 04).

derived.insight: One batch, severity × engine — the full-physics engines show the severity response and agree.

studies.name: 03-workflows
studies.title: Model Orchestration — composable workflows across models, tools, and execution systems
studies.question:
Can the simulation core compose registered modules into a workflow and hand an
Antimony/SBML file between engines — all through a small, uniform API, with no new
simulation code?

parent_studies.rationale: Orchestration composes the interchangeable modules into a workflow.

findings.summary: An Antimony/SBML file handed between engines, composed as a workflow, run with four verbs.
findings.detail:
The BioGears sepsis core was extracted to a portable Antimony/SBML file
(biogears_sepsis.ant). The hand-off workflow (run/handoff_result.json):
  1. LISTS the registered modules (the engine boxes available);
  2. CALLS one — TelluriumUTCStep on the real biogears_sepsis.ant: the SBML/Antimony
     file is loaded and run, the artifact handed from the BioGears C++ engine to the
     Tellurium/roadrunner integrator;
  3. CONNECTS a workflow — the artifact-loading Tellurium node (which runs the real
     model and whose MAP drives the result), a NeuralProcess surrogate tier over
     the same spec, and a MathExpressionStep that derives a clinical shock margin;
  4. RUNS it end-to-end in a few seconds. The handed-off file produces a REAL
     result — the exact Tellurium MAP of biogears_sepsis.ant (~95 mmHg, physical) —
     and the run reports a genuine exact-vs-surrogate MAP comparison (the large gap
     is the honest reminder that the surrogate is a fast approximate tier, study 04/05).
Every node is an existing registered module; nothing in the composition is
sepsis-specific plumbing. The DAG (chart 01) shows the hand-off: a portable model
artifact is the interface between engines, and the exact engine drives the output.
findings.explanation:
The four-verb path ran against real artifacts, not a mock. list enumerated 76 registered modules (engine boxes including TelluriumUTCStep, NeuralProcess, MathExpressionStep). call loaded the extracted biogears_sepsis.ant into TelluriumUTCStep (loaded_ok, ~3.0 s). connect wired a three-node DAG (exact Tellurium / neural surrogate / math derivation). run advanced the composite to finite emitted observables. The handed-off file produced a physical result — a final MAP of 95.54 mmHg under the exact roadrunner integrator. So the portable Antimony/SBML artifact is a working interface between the BioGears-derived core and an SBML solver, with no sepsis-specific plumbing in the composition. That makes the orchestration claim an infrastructure result, not a one-off script.

One scoped caveat on the wording: the end-to-end workflow wall was 125.2 s, not 'a few seconds'. Only the single Tellurium call was ~3.0 s. The 'few seconds' framing mixes per-engine load time with full-pipeline wall and should be read as per-call, not per-workflow; the recorded wall_ms settles it, and a timing test that asserts call wall and run wall separately would pin it down.

The exact-minus-surrogate MAP gap of 95.43 mmHg (surrogate 0.11 vs exact 95.54) and the derived shock margin of -64.89 are not a fidelity failure of the workflow. The surrogate is a deliberately fast, approximate tier whose calibration is the subject of studies 04/05, so the orchestration claim stands on its own, independent of the surrogate's accuracy.

findings.summary: A Nextflow pipeline fans the real sepsis composite across a severity grid — vivarium inside a standard workflow engine.
findings.detail:
Beyond the in-process four-verb workflow, the same composite drops into an
external workflow engine with no special glue. examples/nextflow/sepsis.nf is a
Nextflow DSL2 pipeline: a SEPSIS_RUN task runs the real sepsis_sbml composite
once per severity via `viva-sim run sepsis_sbml --param severity=<N> --emit
parameters/MAP,parameters/TI,parameters/PB` (the same built-in entrypoint the
rest of the core uses), and a SUMMARIZE task gathers every task's final state
into one clinical table (sepsis_summary.tsv), scoring each severity for septic
shock (MAP < 65). The layers are complementary, not competing: Nextflow owns the
outer data-parallel DAG and provenance across tasks; vivarium owns the in-process
engine composition inside each task (the tight per-tick coupling a task scheduler
cannot express — demonstrated in study 06). The toy MathExpressionStep pipeline
(main.nf) remains as the minimal mechanics example.

studies.claim:
The simulation core composes registered modules into a workflow and hands an
Antimony/SBML file between engines, using the four-verb API and no new simulation
code. The BioGears sepsis core — extracted to the portable file biogears_sepsis.ant —
is handed to the TelluriumUTCStep engine (load the file, run it), composed in one
workflow with a NeuralProcess surrogate tier and a MathExpressionStep derivation,
and run end-to-end in a few seconds. The four verbs (list -> call -> connect -> run)
are the entire surface; the portable artifact is the interface between engines.

derived.insight: An Antimony/SBML file handed between engines, composed as a workflow, run with four verbs.

studies.name: 04-performance
studies.title: Scalable Simulation — performance, acceleration, and fidelity-aware execution
studies.question:
How fast is the simulation core, and where does the compute go? For one matched
48 h sepsis run, what does each engine cost, what dominates that cost, and how much
does the learned surrogate save?

parent_studies.rationale: Performance benchmarks the interchangeable engines on the same spec.

findings.summary: One 48 h run, three engines, 4+ orders of magnitude of compute.
findings.detail:
Matched 48 h severe-sepsis run of the same spec (BioGears + Tellurium from the
committed engine-runtime study; surrogate from the folded-in surrogate work):
  - BioGears 8.2.0 (C++ physiology): ~3.38 h
  - Tellurium exact SBML (roadrunner CVODE): ~2.81 h
  - PyTorch surrogate (576-step rollout): ~0.2 s (~40,000x faster than exact)
The two exact engines are the same order of magnitude and both dominated by the
stiff 91-state ODE solve. The surrogate skips the solve entirely (one forward
pass per step), at the cost of accuracy.
findings.statement: The 4+ order-of-magnitude compute spread is a real, matched-spec measurement, but it is about cost alone. The surrogate's ~40,000x full-run and ~13,000x per-step speedups matter only once the fidelity gate is met. Whether the surrogate is a drop-in replacement is decided in study 05, not here.
findings.explanation:
Three engines run the same 48 h severe-sepsis spec and split into two groups. The two exact engines (BioGears ~3.38 h, Tellurium ~2.81 h) sit within the same order of magnitude because both spend their time on the same stiff 91-state ODE solve. The PyTorch surrogate (~0.2 s) sits four orders below because it replaces that solve with a single forward pass. The live per-step micro-benchmark (~526 ms for one exact CVODE step vs ~0.04 ms for one surrogate pass, ~13,000x) pins the cost to that solve, so the spread comes from mechanism, not measurement noise. The companion finding rules out a faster integrator: the ODE is stiff, so an explicit method is unstable and wrong on the fast cardiovascular states.

This study sits downstream of composition -> ensembles -> workflows. It inherits the spec, the matched run, and the engine wrappers rather than re-deriving them, and it feeds fidelity (study 05). It measures cost under a fixed spec and does not measure correctness.

The speedups are compute-only. They tell you which engine is cheaper, not whether the surrogate can replace the exact SBML path. That question is answered by a different number, held-out trajectory error against the exact engine, which study 05's fidelity validator measures. Until that validator passes, the surrogate is a fast approximate tier. The claim this study supports is narrow: the bottleneck is the stiff solve, and the surrogate removes it, at a cost in accuracy this study does not quantify.

findings.summary: The bottleneck is the stiff ODE solve — a faster integrator is not a lever.
findings.detail:
The sepsis ODE is stiff, so only one solver class works: an implicit stiff method
(CVODE/BDF), already compiled as C inside libroadrunner. An explicit fixed-step
integrator (the kind a from-scratch Rust engine uses) is unstable on the real
model and wrong on the fast cardiovascular states, even at ~173 M steps per 48 h.
Rewriting the integrator in another language is not the speed lever. The levers
are a better or warm-started stiff solver, GPU-parallel patients, or a surrogate.
The composition engine is interchangeable on its own: the SBML composite is
bit-identical under process-bigraph Python and the viva-core Rust engine, so that
swap moves only framework overhead.

findings.summary: The Rust viva-core backend runs the same sepsis composite and reproduces the Python result (within-tolerance).
findings.detail:
The composition engine is interchangeable independently of the solver. We ran the
identical sepsis composite under process-bigraph (Python) and under the Rust
viva-core backend (run_rust_backend.py -> rust_backend.json, 60 ticks × 10 s,
healthy baseline). The two backends agree within tolerance: blood pathogen and
tissue integrity are bit-identical, and the hemodynamic observables match to ~1e-5
(max abs diff ~6.6e-5 on SBP). The ~1e-5 residual is roadrunner's
cold-start-vs-warm effect, not an engine disagreement. Wall-clock: Python ~24.0 s
vs viva-core ~21.4 s (ratio ~1.12). This is an execution-backend swap. Roadrunner
does the stiff ODE math in both, so viva-core just runs the composite graph
(state, scheduling, emit) around the same solver. On a single heavy stiff process
the wall-clock difference is framework overhead, not a faster stiff solve.
viva-core's per-tick advantage shows up on many-process or many-tick composites,
and the stiff solve itself stays fixed (see the stiff-ODE finding). What this arm
shows is backend interchangeability and determinism: same composite, two execution
engines, the same numbers.

findings.summary: Live per-step micro-benchmark: the stiff solve is ~13,000x the surrogate forward pass.
findings.detail:
Reproducible on this machine (bench_live.py, warm): one exact CVODE step of the
real 91-state sepsis model costs ~526 ms, against ~0.04 ms for one surrogate
forward pass — the exact per-step solve is ~13,000x the surrogate's. This is the
per-step view behind the full-run wall-clocks, and it shows directly where the
compute goes: the stiff ODE solve. The surrogate is a fast approximate tier (see
study 05 for the fidelity picture).

findings.summary: Speed without admissibility: on severe sepsis the surrogate leaves physical bounds for 8 of 9 observables.
findings.detail:
Acceleration is only useful where the predictions are admissible. Checking the
committed surrogate severe-arm trajectory (data/real_trajectories.json, at the
surrogate's trained 300 s timestep) against simple physical bounds
(surrogate_admissibility.py -> surrogate_admissibility.json, chart 04): 8 of 9
observables leave admissible ranges. The surrogate reaches MAP ~ -158 mmHg, tissue
integrity ~ -6.1, and negative blood pathogen — all physically impossible. Only SVR
stays in bounds. So on severe sepsis the surrogate is not admissible, let alone
mechanistically accurate: its ~40,000x speed does not help here, and the exact
engine is required. This draws the honest line the performance story needs —
screening-grade speed is only a benefit inside the regime where the surrogate stays
physical. A fair held-out-severity admissibility protocol at the trained timestep is
the pending validator (study 07, criterion SURR-01).

findings.summary: COPASI, a second exact-SBML engine, reproduces Tellurium's severe trajectory to ~5e-4 across all 9 observables, at ~4.7x the wall-clock (chart 03).
findings.detail:
Tellurium (roadrunner/CVODE) is the workspace's main SBML engine. Running the
identical BioGears-sepsis SBML (severe, 2 h) under a second, independent exact-SBML
integrator — COPASI (LSODA), driven through libCOPASI's C++ bindings directly, no
basico/pandas layer — reproduces the same trajectory
(run_copasi_vs_tellurium.py -> copasi_vs_tellurium.json, chart 03): the two engines
agree to a maximum relative difference of 5.0e-4 across all nine shared observables
(blood pathogen and tissue integrity agree to ~1e-8; the worst is SBP at 5e-4). So
the exact-SBML behavior is engine-independent, not a roadrunner artifact — an
independent cross-check on the SBML extraction used throughout the investigation.
The agreement costs more: COPASI took ~784 s versus Tellurium's ~168 s (~4.7x). The
cost is the event-dense model — the per-beat event (study 04's event analysis fires
it ~205k times over 48 h). COPASI evaluates each event through an interpreted math
layer while roadrunner runs LLVM-compiled code; bypassing basico's DataFrame (direct
libCOPASI) and loosening tolerance narrow the gap but do not close it, and the
trigger operator (>= vs >) makes no difference. Tellurium remains the main SBML
engine for the investigation; COPASI is the cross-engine validator.

studies.claim:
For one matched 48 h severe-sepsis run, the same spec spans more than 4 orders of
magnitude of compute. BioGears (C++ physiology) takes ~3.38 h. Tellurium (exact SBML
via roadrunner/CVODE) takes ~2.81 h. The PyTorch surrogate takes ~0.2 s — about
40,000x faster than the exact SBML path. The exact engines spend nearly all of that
time integrating the stiff 91-state ODE. That solve needs an implicit stiff solver
(CVODE), so a faster or Rust explicit integrator cannot speed it up; the real levers
are a better stiff solver, GPU-parallel patients, or a surrogate. The surrogate
replaces the ODE solve with one forward pass. A live per-step micro-benchmark on this
machine measures ~526 ms for one exact CVODE step of the real model against ~0.04 ms
for one surrogate forward pass — the exact per-step cost is ~13,000x the surrogate's.
The surrogate is a fast approximate tier (bounded, not yet clinically accurate), not
a drop-in replacement.

derived.insight: The 4+ order-of-magnitude compute spread is a real, matched-spec measurement, but it is about cost alone. The surrogate's ~40,000x full-run and ~13,000x per-step speedups matter only once the fidelity gate is met. Whether the surrogate is a drop-in replacement is decided in study 05, not here.

studies.name: 05-fidelity
studies.title: Mechanistic Fidelity — agreement, discrepancy, and missing physiology
studies.question:
The capability studies show the same spec running under interchangeable engines.
But do the engines actually agree, and where do they diverge? This is the honest
backbone. The demonstration is credible only if the engines' limits are measured,
not hidden.

parent_studies.rationale: Fidelity tests whether the interchangeable engines actually agree; it finds the hemodynamic divergence.

findings.summary: Where they agree — baseline parity and a near-identical (~0.1%) inflammation core.
findings.detail:
At rest both engines hold the StandardMale baseline within tolerance
(00_baseline_parity). Under infection the inflammation observables match to ~0.1%
in both the mild and severe arms (02_inflammation_match): tissue integrity (min
0.243/0.243 severe) and blood pathogen (peak 330.2/330.6). The extracted Acute
Inflammatory Response is a faithful translation of the engine's.

findings.summary: Where they diverge — the hemodynamic layer, in mechanism and timing.
findings.detail:
The divergence lives entirely in the hemodynamics (01_divergence_heatmap). The
engine fluctuates continuously while the autonomous extraction is near-flat. Under
severe sepsis the two reach MAP<65 shock by opposite routes and in flipped order
(engine hypodynamic, MAP<65 at 69.3 h; extraction hyperdynamic, MAP<65 at 54.1 h).
The functional-difference matrix (03_functional_difference_matrix) maps every
divergence to the BioGears subsystem the extraction omits or leaves inert (nitric
oxide, fever vasodilation, renal/urine, lactate, intracellular water).
findings.statement: The hemodynamic divergence is not transcription noise. It is two internally consistent, opposite shock trajectories: the engine reaches MAP<65 by a hypodynamic low-output route (69.3 h), the extraction by a hyperdynamic vasodilatory route (54.1 h). The ~15 h timing gap — earlier even though the extraction lags ~11 h on systolic pressure — and the engine's continuous fluctuation against the extraction's near-flat profile both point to the vasomotor, fluid, and metabolic subsystems the extraction omits, not to a faithfulness failure in the shared spec.
findings.explanation:
Agreement on the inflammation core to within ~0.1% (tissue integrity, blood pathogen) bounds the extraction's error to the hemodynamic layer. The acute inflammatory response is a faithful translation of the engine's; the closed-loop cardiovascular control is not. That turns the divergence into a testable disagreement. The two engines make different predictions about the same severe patient. The C++ engine predicts low-output shock: output falls and MAP<65 arrives later, at 69.3 h. The extraction predicts vasodilatory shock: peripheral resistance falls and MAP<65 arrives earlier, at 54.1 h, even though its systolic pressure trails by ~11 h. Both cannot be right about the real trajectory, so at least one route is an artifact of what the model carries, and every mapped divergence traces to a subsystem the extraction leaves out or inert (nitric oxide, fever vasodilation, renal/urine fluid handling, lactate, intracellular water).

This leaves one test open: trace the cardiac-output-versus-systemic-vascular-resistance split through the shock crossing across the severity sweep and compare it against the BioGears C++ reference. The engine whose output-vs-resistance partition matches the reference at MAP<65 is the faithful one; the other's shock route is the artifact. On the committed severe runs alone, this study measures that the engines diverge and maps each divergence to an omitted subsystem, but it does not yet settle which shock trajectory is correct. The study-04 surrogate is a further, coarser approximation on top of the extraction. The divergence is real and subsystem-localised; which of the two routes is right is still open.

studies.claim:
The engines agree where the extraction is faithful and diverge where it is not. At
rest both hold the StandardMale baseline. Under infection the inflammation core
(tissue integrity, blood pathogen) matches to within ~0.1% in both the mild and
severe arms. They diverge in the hemodynamic layer. The engine fluctuates
continuously (from its nutrition schedule and full homeostatic control) while the
autonomous extraction is near-flat. Under severe sepsis both reach MAP<65 shock, but
by opposite mechanisms and in flipped order: the engine by a hypodynamic low-output
route (MAP<65 at 69.3 h), the extraction by a hyperdynamic vasodilatory route (MAP<65
at 54.1 h) — ~15 h earlier, even though it lags ~11 h on systolic pressure. Every
divergence maps to a vasomotor, fluid, or metabolic subsystem the extraction omits
(nitric oxide, fever vasodilation, renal fluid handling, lactate, intracellular
water). The surrogate is a further, coarser approximation (study 04): fast, bounded,
not clinically accurate.

derived.insight: Where they agree — baseline parity and a near-identical (~0.1%) inflammation core.

studies.name: 06-cosimulation
studies.title: Dynamic Coupling — bidirectional co-simulation and physiological intervention
studies.question:
Can the simulation core run a genuine co-simulation — two processes that exchange
state on every tick inside one composite — rather than running engines in parallel
and comparing them afterwards (studies 01/02) or as parallel tiers (study 03)?

parent_studies.rationale: Intervention acts on the sepsis mechanism fidelity establishes (detect discrepancy -> test treatment).

findings.summary: A physiology engine and an antibiotic controller co-step in one composite, exchanging state every tick.
findings.detail:
The `sepsis_cosim` composite wires two processes into a feedback loop:
  * physiology — the real BioGears-sepsis core run by the Tellurium engine. It
    writes every global parameter (pathogen PT/PB, MAP, SVR, tissue integrity)
    to the shared `parameters` store each step and reads a `parameters_in`
    writeback before the next step.
  * controller — AntibioticControllerProcess: reads `parameters`, senses the
    blood pathogen PB, integrates a one-compartment antibiotic PK (first-order
    elimination), computes an Emax bactericidal kill, and writes the reduced
    PT/PB back to `parameters_in`.
PT/PB are rate-rule state variables in the SBML, not assignment-rule outputs, so
roadrunner accepts the controller's mid-run writeback and the loop closes on the
real flagship model with no model surgery. This is co-simulation in the strict
sense: the controller's tick-n output is the engine's tick-(n+1) input. The same
composite with treat=False makes the controller inert, giving the matched
untreated control.

findings.summary: Closed-loop antibiotic clears bacteremia; the untreated control's pathogen climbs (see chart 01).
findings.detail:
Run at severity 3 over 2 h (120 ticks; see chart 01 and out/cosim_arms.json). The
untreated arm's blood pathogen rises to ~10.6 and plateaus. The closed-loop arm
drives it to 0 once the controller senses PB crossing its trigger and starts the
infusion (final bacteremia ratio untreated/treated = ∞). The treated arm's
sawtooth is the per-tick coupling made visible: the pathogen regrows within each
physiology step and the controller knocks it back down every tick. The figure also
shows the controller's own live state — antibiotic concentration from its
one-compartment PK, rising to ~5.9, and the sensed treat-on flag — which confirms
the second process is simulating, not scripted. Even at this short horizon a
downstream clinical effect is already visible: untreated tissue integrity has
begun to fall (1.000 -> 0.983) while the treated arm holds at 1.000, the first
measurable tissue damage, prevented by clearing the pathogen. Honest limit: the
clinical endpoint that defines septic shock (MAP < 65 mmHg at ~54 h, tissue
integrity minimum 0.24 at 72 h; studies 03/05) is a 2–3 day process, and the exact
engine runs ~1.75 h of wall per simulated 48 h. So this run's horizon shows the
controlled variable (pathogen) and the live PK — the loop removing the cause of
collapse — not the multi-day outcome itself. A full-horizon treated-vs-untreated
endpoint comparison is the natural follow-up.
findings.statement: This co-simulation demonstrates the mechanism (per-tick state exchange with feedback) and the controlled variable (pathogen clearance), not the multi-day clinical endpoint.
findings.explanation: The main claim is a capability claim, and it is fully supported: two process-bigraph processes run in one composite and exchange state every tick through shared stores, with a genuine feedback edge (the controller's writeback at tick n is the engine's input at tick n+1). That is what sets co-simulation apart from the parallel engine comparison of studies 01/02 (same spec under different engines, compared after the fact) and from the parallel surrogate tier of study 03. The clinical instance — a closed-loop antibiotic that senses bacteremia and doses against it — is chosen so the coupling does something legible: the controller clears the pathogen that the matched untreated control (the identical composite with the controller disabled) lets climb. This study does not claim a validated clinical outcome. The pathogen is the upstream driver of the sepsis cascade (inflammation -> vasodilation -> hypotension), so clearing it removes the cause of collapse, but the collapse itself unfolds over 37-72 h (studies 03/05), and the exact engine is too slow to integrate matched treated/untreated arms to that endpoint in this pass. So the honest reading is: the co-simulation capability is demonstrated end to end on the real model, and the treatment's effect on its direct target (bacteremia) is shown; the downstream multi-day endpoint is referenced from the committed severity studies, not re-derived here. The controller's PK is an illustrative Emax/one-compartment model, not a calibrated pharmacology. Swapping it for a COPASI/Tellurium PK engine (true heterogeneous engine-to-engine co-simulation) is a noted follow-up.

findings.summary: Untreated vs early vs delayed treatment give an ordered, consistent response — earlier is better (see chart 02).
findings.detail:
Three arms from the identical sepsis_cosim composite (severity 3, 2 h; delay 1 h),
differing only in when the controller starts (run_counterfactuals.py ->
out/cosim_counterfactuals.json):
  * untreated — bacteremia climbs to 10.6; tissue integrity ends 0.9828.
  * delayed treatment (onset 1 h) — bacteremia tracks the untreated arm for the
    first hour, then drops sharply once treatment starts, ending 0.162; tissue
    integrity ends 0.9874.
  * early treatment (onset at detection) — bacteremia is cleared (ends 0.006);
    tissue integrity holds at 1.0000.
The ordering is consistent: earlier treatment clears the pathogen sooner and
leaves more tissue intact (early 1.0000 > delayed 0.9874 > untreated 0.9828 at 2 h).
The tissue-integrity gaps are small at this horizon because the clinical collapse
is a multi-day process; the pathogen trajectories separate the three arms cleanly.
This is a treatment counterfactual, not a dosing recommendation: the PK is
illustrative, not calibrated.

findings.summary: The co-simulation is numerically consistent: the endpoint converges as the coupling step shrinks.
findings.detail:
Running the early-treatment arm at shrinking coupling steps (240 / 120 / 60 s per
tick, 1 h; out/cosim_convergence.json) gives final bacteremia 0.4115 / 0.3747 /
0.3566 — monotone and converging, a total spread of 0.0548 across a 4× change in
step size (small against the untreated arm's ~10.6). The one-tick coupling lag
shrinks with the step, as expected for operator-split co-simulation. This separates
execution success (the coupling runs and converges) from pharmacological credibility
(the controller's PK is illustrative, not calibrated).

studies.claim:
The `sepsis_cosim` composite couples two process-bigraph processes that exchange
state every tick. The Tellurium sepsis physiology engine writes its global parameters
(pathogen, hemodynamics) to a shared store. An antibiotic-PK controller process reads
the pathogen, integrates a one-compartment drug PK, and writes the drug-killed
pathogen back into the engine through its `parameters_in` port before the engine's
next step. The treatment the controller computes at tick n changes the physiology the
engine integrates at tick n+1 — a real feedback loop, not two independent runs. With
the controller enabled (closed-loop antibiotic), bacteremia is cleared. With it
disabled (treat=False, the matched control from the same composite), bacteremia
climbs. The pathogen drives septic collapse, so the loop removes the cause. The
multi-day clinical endpoint itself (studies 03/05) is beyond this run's horizon.

derived.insight: A physiology engine and an antibiotic controller co-step in one composite, exchanging state every tick.

studies.name: 07-evidence
studies.title: Scientific Evidence & Acceptance — from simulation runs to reproducible claims
studies.question:
Can the Workbench turn simulation outputs into traceable evidence, evaluate explicit
acceptance criteria, tell supported claims from unsupported ones, and flag the
verification still needed?

parent_studies.rationale: Evaluates the fidelity discrepancy as acceptance criteria.
Evaluates the intervention evidence (discrepancy -> counterfactual -> evidence).

findings.summary: Four pre-declared criteria evaluate to 2 pass, 1 fail, 1 pending — each traced to evidence (see chart 01).
findings.detail:
evaluate_acceptance.py reads the committed study-05 milestones
(02-ensembles/data/{engine,sbml}-sev3.milestones.json), applies each criterion's
declared tolerance, and writes out/acceptance_eval.json:
  * INFLAM-01 pass — minimum tissue integrity: engine 0.243052 vs SBML 0.243042,
    relative error 0.0044% (tolerance 1%).
  * INFLAM-02 pass — peak blood pathogen: engine 330.20 vs SBML 330.60,
    relative error 0.12% (tolerance 1%).
  * HEMO-01 fail — time to MAP < 65 mmHg: engine 69.3 h vs SBML 54.1 h, 15.3 h
    apart (tolerance 6 h). This is the known hemodynamic divergence from study 05,
    now expressed as a failed, evidence-linked acceptance criterion.
  * SURR-01 pending — surrogate hemodynamic accuracy within 10% of the exact engine:
    the criterion is declared, but the held-out surrogate-vs-exact validator has not
    been run, so it is reported pending, not passed.
The split is the point: the inflammation core passes, the hemodynamic layer fails,
and the surrogate's clinical accuracy is an open verification need. Each verdict
links back to the exact artifact (or names the missing test), so the claims are
traceable rather than asserted.

findings.summary: The study's scientific verdict is reconciled with its pending acceptance metadata, not quietly rewritten.
findings.detail:
This study's own verdict is 'supported' for one specific claim: the acceptance
machinery runs and produces linked pass/fail/pending verdicts. That is separate
from the scientific status of the sepsis model itself, which the gates report
honestly — the hemodynamic criterion fails and the surrogate criterion is pending.
A completed demonstration verdict and an open acceptance gate coexist here on
purpose: the Workbench records the pending gate rather than inflating the verdict to
mask it.
findings.statement: Study 07 demonstrates the acceptance method, not a clean bill of health for the sepsis model.
findings.explanation: The supported verdict is scoped to the method: committed evidence flows through declared criteria to traceable pass/fail/pending verdicts, with at least one of each, each linked to an artifact or a named missing test. It does not claim the sepsis model passes overall. Two of its gates do not: HEMO-01 fails (the hemodynamic divergence from study 05) and SURR-01 is pending (the surrogate accuracy validator is unrun). Reporting those honestly, beside a completed demonstration verdict, is the behavior the study is meant to show. The follow-up that would close SURR-01 is a held-out, multi-seed surrogate-vs-exact trajectory comparison (study 04); the follow-up that would turn HEMO-01 into an explained result rather than a bare failure is the mechanistic perturbation test (study 05).

studies.claim:
The Workbench evaluates pre-declared acceptance criteria against committed evidence
and records a traceable verdict for each. Using the study-05 severe-arm milestones as
the evidence source (evaluate_acceptance.py -> out/acceptance_eval.json), four criteria
were declared with tolerances and evaluated: INFLAM-01 (minimum tissue integrity agrees
to within 1%) passes at 0.0044% relative error; INFLAM-02 (peak blood pathogen within
1%) passes at 0.12%; HEMO-01 (time to MAP < 65 mmHg agrees within 6 h) fails at 15.3 h
apart (engine 69.3 h vs SBML 54.1 h); and SURR-01 (surrogate hemodynamic accuracy within
10% of the exact engine) is pending — its validator has not been run. Two pass, one fail,
one pending, each linked to its evidence artifact or its missing-evidence note.

derived.insight: Four pre-declared criteria evaluate to 2 pass, 1 fail, 1 pending — each traced to evidence (see chart 01).

studies.name: 08-reduced-model
studies.title: Model Reduction — event-driven vs event-free (speed vs fidelity)
studies.question:
The per-beat event (E_beat) fires ~205k times over 48 h and is ~99% of the full
model's runtime. Can we replace the events with a continuous mean-hemodynamics model
that still reproduces the sepsis trajectory — and how much faster, and at what cost
to fidelity?

parent_studies.rationale: Performance localized the cost to the per-beat event; this study removes it.
Tests how much hemodynamic fidelity is lost when the pulsatile event layer is dropped.

findings.summary: Event-free: ~0.2 ms (roadrunner) / ~0.06 ms (COPASI) for 48 h vs ~2.81 h / ~3.7 h full — ~10^7-10^8x, and COPASI = roadrunner (see chart 02).
findings.detail:
The full pulsatile model's ~205k beat events are ~99% of its runtime (study 04:
disabling the event dropped a 60 s COPASI run from 3.8 s to 0.04 s). The event-free
reduced model has no events and is non-stiff, so a 48 h course runs in ~0.2 ms
(roadrunner) and ~0.06 ms (COPASI), against ~2.81 h (roadrunner) and ~3.7 h (COPASI)
for the full model — a ~6x10^7 / ~2x10^8 speedup (out/comparison.json). Crucially,
with the events gone COPASI is as fast as roadrunner (slightly faster here): the
~3x Tellurium-vs-COPASI gap was entirely the per-event interpreter overhead, so it
disappears when there are no events.

findings.summary: The reduced model tracks pathogen (~10%), tissue integrity (~4%), and the MAP decline (~4% RMSE), but under-reaches shock and misses the SVR compensation (chart 01).
findings.detail:
Fitted to the exact severe arm (data/real_trajectories.json), the event-free model
(chart 01, out/comparison.json) tracks blood pathogen to ~10% RMSE, tissue integrity
to ~4%, and the mean-MAP decline to ~4%. The fidelity cost is specific and visible:
the full model's SVR is non-monotonic — it rises to ~1.12 (baroreflex vasoconstriction,
compensation) before crashing to 0.665 (decompensation) — whereas the reduced model's
SVR falls monotonically, so it ends at ~0.78 vs 0.665 and MAP at ~80 vs 69.5 mmHg. It
captures the direction and most of the shock but not its full depth or the
two-phase hemodynamic response, and it has no pulsatility (no SBP/DBP pulse pressure).
So the reduced model is a screening-grade surrogate for the slow sepsis outcome, not a
replacement for the pulsatile physiology.
findings.statement: The event-free model is a speed/fidelity trade, not a free lunch: ~10^7x faster and engine-agnostic, at the cost of hemodynamic depth, the baroreflex SVR dynamics, and pulsatility.
findings.explanation: The removed structure and the lost fidelity are the same thing. The per-beat event is what makes the full model both expensive (205k root-finds + reinits, ~99% of runtime) and detailed (beat-to-beat pulse pressure, and the baroreflex that drives SVR up before it collapses). Dropping it buys ~10^7x speed and removes the per-event interpreter overhead that made COPASI ~3x slower — so the engines converge. It costs the pulsatile layer (no SBP/DBP) and the compensation-then-decompensation SVR trajectory, which a monotonic mean-hemodynamics model cannot represent; hence the reduced model under-reaches the shock depth even after fitting. The honest placement: this is a fast screening surrogate for the slow sepsis outcome (pathogen, tissue integrity, mean-MAP trend), useful where thousands of runs or interactive exploration matter, and the full pulsatile model remains the reference where hemodynamic depth, pulse pressure, or the baroreflex dynamics matter. A closer fit would need a two-phase (compensation) hemodynamic term, a noted follow-up.

studies.claim:
Removing the per-beat event and the pulsatile layer makes the 48 h sepsis run
~10^7-10^8x faster and closes the COPASI-vs-Tellurium gap. The event-free model
(sources/eventfree_sepsis.ant) runs a 48 h severe course in ~0.2 ms under roadrunner
and ~0.06 ms under COPASI, versus ~2.81 h (roadrunner) and ~3.7 h (COPASI) for the
full model — and with the events gone COPASI is as fast as roadrunner, because the
~3x engine gap was entirely per-event interpreter overhead. Fitted to the exact
severe arm, the reduced model tracks blood pathogen to ~10%, tissue integrity to
~4%, and the mean-MAP decline to ~4% RMSE. It trades fidelity for that speed: it
under-reaches the shock depth (MAP ~80 vs 69.5 mmHg; SVR ~0.78 vs 0.665) and, being
monotonic, misses the full model's baroreflex SVR compensation-then-decompensation,
and it has no pulsatility (no SBP/DBP pulse pressure).

derived.insight: Event-free: ~0.2 ms (roadrunner) / ~0.06 ms (COPASI) for 48 h vs ~2.81 h / ~3.7 h full — ~10^7-10^8x, and COPASI = roadrunner (see chart 02).
